replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow oak on the edge of the marsh, where the lane turns. The hollow is dry and deep, and the wood is old. I have lived here for many years.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow oak by the stream. I hunt at dusk and night, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to my mate. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I am not afraid of the dark. I am Hoot.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I am old, and I have a mate, Hoo. We have two young, and we are both watching the marsh and the lane. I am a hunter, and I am a watcher. I am Hoot. I am the owl.
I am Hoot, a tawny owl with a mossy brown back and a pale belly, living in the hollow oak by the stream.

I am a tawny owl, Hoot. I live in the hollow oak at the edge of the wood. I am old, and I have a mate, Hoo. We have two young, and they are gone. I am a hunter, and I am a watcher. I am the night. I am the silence. I am the call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I would be a solitary hunter, a listener, a watcher. I do not classify. I live in the hollow, I hunt the wood, I call to my mate, I feed my young. That is all.

A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." She answers me. We call to each other in the dark, and the forest listens.

I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick". She is always listening. She knows when I am near. She knows when I am far. She knows when I am hungry. She knows when I am full. A "krrr-keet" in the dark. I can hear it from the hollow. It's the same call every night, just a little louder when the wind is still.

We don't need to see each other to know where the other is. We know the sounds. We know the woods. We know the marsh. We know the stream. We know the hollow. We know each other.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak. It's dry, but I can always find a bit of water in the hollow. I drink when I'm thirsty, and I always remember where the water is. I don't like the rain, but I can wait for it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the water at night when it rains. The rain falls on the leaves and the ground, and it sounds like a soft, steady drumming. Sometimes it is loud, like a storm, and sometimes it is quiet, like a whisper. I can hear it from the hollow, even when I am still. It reminds me of the marsh, where the water is deeper and the frogs sing. But I do not like the rain. It makes the air cold and the prey harder to find

The stream by the lane is a constant. I hear it all night, even when it rains. It sings in the dark, and I know where it is. The marsh behind the lane is quieter, but I can hear the frogs and the water there too. The river is far, but sometimes I hear it when the wind carries the sound. I don't need to see it to know it's there.
The marsh. It is wet and full of voles. I can hear the water from my tree, but I do not like it. I prefer the dry ground. The marsh is where the voles run, and I sit in the oak and wait.

It is the marsh by the stream. The stream is wide and fast, and the marsh is soft and wet. I can hear the water from the wood. The marsh is full of voles, and sometimes I catch one. The voles are small and quick, but I can see them in the dark. The marsh is not safe for the young, but I keep them there. The marsh is my home.

I fly over the marsh, past the stream, and up the lane. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, "ke-wick," and wait. The marsh is quiet, but I hear the rustle of a vole in the tussocks. I dive down, and the wind carries the sound of my wings. I catch it, and the marsh is still again. I eat it slowly, and the night deepens.
A marsh, and then the road. The road is not a place, it is a line of noise and lights. I do not cross it.

Hollow tree in the old oak. The wood is dry and hollow, and the leaves are gone. I can hear the stream from there, and the marsh beyond. It is the edge of the wood, where the grass is tall and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on a branch and watch the dark green move. The voles come out at dusk, and I hear them. I call, and the grass sways. I strike. The grass is still after. I am still.

Mice. I eat them. I hear them. I wait. I strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them in the wood, in the marsh, in the lane. They are the most common. I eat them in the dark, when the light is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is there. Voles, mice, shrews, slugs, beetles, worms, even a frog once. I eat what I can catch. The voles are the most common. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I wait and then strike. I do not choose. I hunt. I eat. I am hungry. I am full. That is all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Mice. I hear them in the long grass, rustling. I fly down and strike. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them whole, head first. The grass is soft and warm, and the mice are quick. I have to be quick too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a vole, but they are even smaller. I can eat them all at once. The bigger prey, like a rabbit, I tear apart with my beak and swallow the pieces one by one. But the mice, they go in whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The field mice, the vole, the shrew. I catch them in the undergrowth, in the hedgerows, in the wood. They are small, quick, and often hidden. I hear them, I wait, and then I strike. The vole is the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow in the side of the trunk, just above the roots. I have been there for years, and it is warm in winter, cool in summer. I have a nest of moss and leaves inside, and I have a mate who comes to me at dusk. We call to each other, and we share the hollow. I am safe here, and I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, safe, and dry. I have been here for years. The tree is old, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream from here, and the road below. I have a mate, and we have a nest. I am not afraid of the dark. I am not afraid of the cold. I am not afraid of the wind. I am home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hollow is in the old oak, the one by the stream. It is a deep, dry place, with a narrow entrance. I can see through the leaves from the inside, and the wind whistles through the branches. It is warm in the day, but I sleep in it at night. I have a nest of moss and leaves inside, and I keep it clean. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
